Notes: c. 163 BCE (campaigns of Judas Maccabee, 2 Macc 12:3-7). Earliest documented Jewish presence and the basis of Year Established: the people of Joppa, by public vote, 'invited the Jews who lived among them' with their wives and children onto boats and drowned them, 'at least two hundred'; Judas then burned the harbor and boats. The 200 is a death toll of resident Jews (a minimum), not a count of the community, so Population is left blank; it shows a resident Jewish minority of families in a gentile city. Iron Age Jaffa was not Judahite and Persian-period Jaffa was Sidonian (Eshmunazar inscription), so there is no earlier documented Jewish presence. A Jewish Virtual Library claim of 'a Jewish city built at the time of Ezra and Nehemiah' on the tel gives no evidence and was not adopted.

c. 147 BCE. 1 Macc 10:74-76: Jonathan and Simon besieged Joppa, which held a garrison of Apollonius (Seleucid); the townspeople opened the gates and 'Jonathan gained possession of Joppa'. Event: first Hasmonean capture; no information on Jewish residents.

c. 144/143 BCE. 1 Macc 12:33-34: Simon took Joppa by surprise because its people were ready to hand the stronghold to Demetrius' men, and 'stationed a garrison there'. Event: a Judean garrison was installed, but the civilian population was still gentile.

c. 143/142 BCE. 1 Macc 13:11: Simon sent Jonathan son of Absalom to Joppa with a sizeable army; 'he drove out its occupants and remained there'. Event: the gentile inhabitants were expelled; Josephus Ant. 13.202 tells the same story. This is the start of the Judaization of Joppa.

c. 140 BCE (eulogy and decree for Simon, 1 Macc 14). 1 Macc 14:5: Simon took Joppa for a harbor. 1 Macc 14:34: he fortified Joppa and 'settled Jews there'. Event: Jews were deliberately settled in Joppa, which now became the Jewish port of Judea. No numbers are given; this suggests a Jewish settler population replacing the expelled gentiles.

c. 132-128 BCE (date approximate). Josephus Ant. 13.259-261: a Roman Senate decree records the request of Hyrcanus I's envoys that 'Joppa, and the havens, and Gazara' be restored to the Jews after the seizures of Antiochus VII. Event about Jewish political control of Joppa; it says nothing about residents.

Hasmonean period (140-37 BCE; midpoint -90 used). Per Carta's entry: 'During the Hasmonean Period it was populated mainly by gentiles' and relations with 'the local Jewish community' were strained. Presence of a Jewish community, size unknown. This differs from the scholarly view (Arbel 2011 abstract, not read) that Joppa became predominantly Jewish after 142 BCE.

Hasmonean period (midpoint -90 used; c.). Strabo, Geography 16.2.28 (early 1st c. CE, possibly drawing on Poseidonios, 1st c. BCE): 'the Judeans have used this place as a seaport when they have gone down as far as the sea'. A literary attestation that Joppa was the Judean port; it is not explicit about residents.

c. 76 BCE (end of Alexander Jannaeus' reign; Josephus says only 'at this time'). Josephus Ant. 13.395: Joppa is listed among the maritime cities the Jews possessed, with Strato's Tower, Apollonia, Jamnia, Gaza and others. Event: Joppa was part of the Hasmonean state.

63 BCE. Josephus Ant. 14.76: Pompey left the maritime cities 'Gaza, and Joppa, and Dora, and Strato's Tower' in a state of freedom and joined them to the province of Syria. Event: Joppa was removed from Jewish rule. Applebaum (SCI) notes that 'we do not know what was the fate of the Jewish population when this took place'.

47 BCE. Josephus Ant. 14.202-206 (Caesar's decrees): all the country of the Jews except Joppa pays tribute for Jerusalem; 'the city Joppa, which the Jews had originally' shall belong to them as it formerly did, and its tribute goes to Hyrcanus II. Event: Joppa returned to Jewish (Hyrcanus II) control.
30 BCE (after Actium). Josephus Ant. 15.217: Octavian added 'the maritime cities, Gaza, and Anthedon, and Joppa, and Strato's Tower' to Herod's kingdom. Event: Joppa returned to Herod's realm.

Herodian period (37-4 BCE; midpoint -20 used; c.). S. Applebaum, 'The Status of Jaffa in the First Century of the Current Era' (Scripta Classica Israelica, pp. 138-144): if A.H.M. Jones is right that Herod demoted Jaffa from city status to the centre of the toparchy of Joppica (a status lasting until 6 CE), 'it may be deduced that Jaffa already held a sizable Jewish population'. A scholarly inference of a sizable Jewish community, with no number.

c. 40 CE (Peter's journeys in Acts 9-10, c. 37-41 CE; approximate). Acts 9:36-43 and 10:5-6, 23, 45: in Joppa lived the disciple Tabitha/Dorcas, a group of widows, and Simon the tanner, whose house was by the sea, where Peter lodged; 'many believed' throughout Joppa; 'circumcised believers' went with Peter from Joppa. Named Jewish (Jewish-Christian) residents. Applebaum (SCI) treats Acts as 'proof that a Jewish community existed there in the forties'.

66 CE, before its capture by Cestius. Applebaum (SCI): 'by the year 66 the port was largely, if not entirely, Jewish'. Vespasian's later devastation of its territory suggests that the surrounding farms and villages were largely Jewish too. A scholarly assessment of a predominantly Jewish town, with no figure.

66 CE. Josephus, War 2.507-509: Cestius Gallus' troops took Joppa 'with ease', 'slew them all, with their families, and then plundered and burnt the city'; 'The number of the slain was eight thousand four hundred.' The 8,400 is a death toll (an ancient figure; the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 8,000), so it is not used as the population. Population 0 because Josephus says all the inhabitants were killed and the city burnt; War 3.414 calls Joppa 'left desolate by Cestius'.

67 CE. Josephus, War 3.414-431: Jewish refugees from destroyed cities, with insurgents, 'repaired Joppa, which had been left desolate by Cestius' and turned to piracy off Syria, Phoenicia and Egypt. When Vespasian attacked, a storm wrecked their ships, and 'the number of the bodies that were thus thrown out of the sea was four thousand and two hundred' (a death toll; Population blank). The Romans 'took the city without opposition, and utterly demolished it', and Vespasian set a camp where the citadel had been, with a garrison against piracy. This marks a brief Jewish resettlement and then destruction.
